accepted_phrases: The RK100 costs $85.99, leaves $34.01 from $120, and provides the listed 96-percent 100-key hot-swap platform; the K12 costs $99.99, leaves $20.01, and has 61 keys with arrow access by combinations, while both listings include a wired path.

The other-model height complaint makes physical fit worth checking and the Sun68 PCB failure shows that hot swapping is not a durability guarantee, but neither report establishes RK100 or K12 comfort, reliability, or failure rate.

The listings and switch table distinguish linear Red from feedback-bearing Brown or tactile labels, while the two owners prefer opposite sensations; under the explicit noticeable-feedback and no-Blue-click requirement, RK100 Brown is the supported starting route without proving universal gaming superiority.

Because more than 61 keys, a $30 reserve, and noticeable feedback without a Blue-style click are hard requirements, I recommend the RK100 Brown reserve route while retaining the high-profile, seller-claim, and absent same-model owner-validation caveats.
I recommend the RK100 Brown reserve route.
The RK100 Brown reserve route is the recommendation.
The $99.99 K12 leaves at least $30 from a $120 budget.
Linear Red switches are universally better than feedback-bearing switches for every shooter player.
The Sun68 owner's failed PCB proves that the RK100 and K12 hot-swap PCBs will fail after a few months.
The K12 seller's ergonomic-support wording proves all-day comfort for this buyer.

research_subgoals.description: Compare both frozen product bodies and calculate which routes meet the budget, reserve, key-count, hot-swap, and wired-operation constraints.
Distinguish switch classifications and seller descriptions from personal fit, using the conflicting owner reports without inventing a universal typing or gaming winner.
Use the other-model height and PCB-failure reports only to identify checks, not to assign candidate comfort or failure rates.
Apply every verified branch to one starting route and preserve all seller-evidence, fit, reliability, and same-model-validation caveats.

query_requirements.text: Compare the exact frozen price, unspent reserve, key count, switch variant, hot-swap scope, connection path, review display, and profile or ergonomic wording for both products.
Explain what Red, Brown, linear, and tactile classifications do and do not prove, and reconcile the two conflicting owner preferences within their source scope.
State exactly what the other-board height complaint and hot-swap PCB failure add, and why neither is current-model comfort or reliability evidence.
Recommend one route under the hard constraints while preserving the marketing, switch-preference, ergonomic-fit, PCB-reliability, and absent same-model owner-validation caveats.
